questions.q: What is the main purpose of an escalation policy?
options: To punish on-call engineers who miss a page
To define what happens when an alert goes unacknowledged, so it re-routes instead of dying silently
To decide which engineer is best at fixing a given bug
To replace the need for an on-call rotation entirely
questions.explain: An escalation policy exists because people miss pages — it defines the next step (secondary on-call, then a lead) so an unacknowledged alert doesn't just go unanswered.

questions.q: A regional outage affects a meaningful but partial slice of customers. Which severity level does this most likely map to?
options: SEV4, since it isn't affecting everyone
SEV1, since any customer impact requires an all-hands page
SEV2, since it's significant but partial impact rather than widespread
SEV3, because workarounds always exist for regional issues
questions.explain: SEV2 describes significant but partial impact (such as one region or some users), distinct from SEV1's widespread impact or SEV3/SEV4's minor/no customer impact.

questions.q: Why is the incident commander role kept separate from the engineer actively debugging the issue?
options: Because the IC is always more senior and shouldn't do hands-on work
Because coordinating communication and tracking the response are different cognitive tasks than deep technical investigation, and combining them slows both down
Because company policy requires two people on every incident
Because the IC role doesn't require any technical background
questions.explain: The IC coordinates — tracking time, owning communication, deciding on escalation — while the investigating engineer focuses on diagnosis. Combining both in one person degrades both tasks.

questions.q: During a customer-visible SEV1, why would a team post a status page update saying 'we're investigating' before they know the root cause?
options: Because silence during a visible outage erodes customer trust faster than an honest acknowledgment that investigation is underway
Because status pages are legally required within one minute of any incident
Because it removes the need for an incident commander
Because customers prefer technical detail over reassurance
questions.explain: An early, honest 'we're investigating' update is better than silence, even without a root cause yet — it maintains trust during a visible outage.

questions.q: What is the practical risk of under-calling a real SEV1 incident as a SEV3?
options: None — severity labels are just for internal record-keeping
It costs response time that can't be recovered, because fewer people get paged and no incident commander is assigned early
It automatically triggers a postmortem regardless of actual impact
It only affects how the status page is worded
questions.explain: Severity determines who gets paged, whether a commander is assigned, and whether a status page update goes out — under-calling severity delays all of that at the moment it matters most.
